Ought
ât
v. (to be bound in duty; rendering Greek dei and opheilo)
The old past tense of owe: what one ought is what one owes. The word carries the whole grammar of moral obligation in five letters.

Biblical Definition

Ought names moral debt. The apostles wield it against every rival claim — “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — and the risen Lord uses it of His own path: “Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?” (Luk 24:26). It binds worship's details — “these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone” (Mat 23:23) — and it bends the church toward the basin: “ye also ought to wash one another's feet” (Joh 13:14). Obligation, in Scripture, is owed love with its sleeves rolled up.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ought as to be held or bound in duty or moral obligation, citing this very verse — these ought ye to have done.

expand to see more

OUGHT, v. imperfect. To be held or bound in duty or moral obligation. Matt. 23.

2. To be necessary; to behoove.

Key Scripture

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Luk 24:26 — "Ought not Christ to have suffered these things, and to enter into his glory?"

Mat 23:23 — "Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye pay tithe of mint and anise and cummin, and have omitted the weightier matters of the law, judgment, mercy, and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone."

Joh 13:14 — "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet."

Modern Corruption

A culture allergic to ought — obligation rebranded as trauma, duty dissolved into authenticity — while Scripture grounds the sweetest realities, from Christ's cross to washed feet, in holy necessity.

expand to see more

The modern self recognizes no debts it did not choose, so ought survives only as oppression's vocabulary. But the Emmaus road hangs redemption itself on the word: ought not Christ to have suffered? — a necessity rooted in covenant and prophecy, which the Son embraced freely and called His meat. Where ought is abolished, love loses its spine; the New Testament's obligations are love's owed shape: owe no man any thing, but to love one another.

Acts 5:29 marks the word's political edge. When commands collide, obligation stacks: we ought to obey God rather than men — not instead of men, but rather, a ranked debt. The church that has forgotten how to say ought will discover, when the collision comes, that it has nothing to stand on but preference — and preference folds.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek dei (G1163), it is necessary — the must of Christ's sufferings; opheilo (G3784), to owe — the debt-word of washed feet and mutual love.

expand to see more

Greek dei (G1163) — it is necessary, one must; ought not Christ to have suffered (Luk 24:26); ye must be born again (Joh 3:7).

Greek opheilo (G3784) — to owe, be indebted; ye also ought to wash one another's feet (Joh 13:14); we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren (1Jn 3:16).

Usage

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” — obligations rank, and God outranks."

"“Ought not Christ to have suffered these things?” — redemption ran on holy necessity."

"“Ye also ought to wash one another's feet” — owed love with a towel on."
